time.desc: The leader of one party questioned the status of the opponent's most powerful figure in public interviews and social platforms, and claimed to have sent a letter requesting negotiations on nuclear issues and threatening military consequences. The opponent's government publicly responded by refusing to give in under threats and denying relevant rumors.

A senior economic official from one side expressed his position on the navigation of the strategic strait, saying that he would not object to the passage of ships from some countries for the time being, and directly linked whether to adjust the energy market response to the duration of the conflict.
One side of the conflict confirmed that its key senior official was killed in an airstrike by the other side, becoming one of the highest-ranking officials killed since the war began.

The coalition launched a new round of air strikes on energy infrastructure such as large natural gas fields on one side of the conflict, triggering a significant market reaction to energy supply risks.

The leader of one side issued a time-limited ultimatum, requiring the opponent to resume commercial shipping in the strategic strait, otherwise it will attack the opponent's key civilian energy facilities such as power generation.

The military of one party to the conflict stated that if the opponent carries out its threat to attack energy facilities, it will take measures to completely close the strategic strait as a countermeasure.

One party announced that it had opened dialogue with its opponent and promised to suspend attacks on its energy facilities for a few days. Officials of the opponent confirmed that negotiations were ongoing.
One side formally submitted a multi-provisional plan to end the conflict to its opponent in an attempt to promote a ceasefire and deal with the strategic strait crisis.
The opponent completed a formal written reply to the multi-term ceasefire plan, and the ceasefire negotiations entered a new stage.
The two parties carried out joint attacks on important port facilities close to the strategic strait and caused casualties.

The two countries outside the region jointly proposed a plan to end the war containing several points, calling for an immediate ceasefire and the restoration of normal traffic in the strategic strait.
In a nationally televised address, the leader of one side announced tougher military strikes against its rivals in the coming weeks and reiterated hope for a shorter cutoff to end the conflict.

The two sides launched joint air strikes against their opponents' key petrochemical industrial parks and facilities near export ports, further expanding the scope of their attacks on the energy industry chain.

The leader of one side publicly threatened to bomb the opponent's civilian infrastructure such as power plants and bridges by name and demanded the opening of the strait; the opponent's senior adviser warned that he would retaliate by blocking another key sea channel.
One side agreed to suspend bombings and attacks on its opponents for two weeks, forming a clear ceasefire window and significantly affecting energy market expectations.

Relevant parties publicly clarified that the ceasefire arrangement did not cover their military operations against third-party armed forces, triggering diplomatic disagreements over whether the scope of application of the ceasefire should be expanded.

The opponent's country held commemorative activities for the most powerful person before he was killed; at the same time, the idea of ​​charging fees for strategic strait passage caused controversy and became one of the focus of negotiations.
The military of one party officially launched a naval blockade of the opponent's port and stated that it would not prevent ships related to non-rival ports from passing through the strategic strait.
The leader of the attacking party publicly called on all countries to go to the key straits to rush for oil, claiming that the attacked party had basically been defeated.
